analysis.one_liner: Bans slicing fins off sharks and dumping the body back into the ocean, with import bans on finning nations.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill, introduced by Sen. John Kerry with one cosponsor in June 2000, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there without a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime under the nation's main fishing law to engage in shark-finning — cutting off a shark's valuable fins and dumping the rest of the body back into the sea — and to land fins taken that way. It would presume fins on a fishing vessel came from finning unless the operator proves otherwise, ban imports of shark fins from countries that lack comparable anti-finning rules, require annual reports on nations that allow finning, fund shark research, and direct diplomats to push for a worldwide finning ban.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a stake in healthy oceans: shark populations, which grow slowly and are easily wiped out by finning; commercial and recreational fishers who depend on stable shark stocks; coastal communities tied to marine life; and consumers, since the bill bans the practice of wasting roughly 95 percent of each shark caught for a 5-percent fin. It also funds research with the fishing industry on gear that avoids catching sharks in the first place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ocean health and coastal fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: Makes shark-finning — removing fins and discarding the carcass — and landing fins taken that way unlawful under the Magnuson-Stevens Act, closing a loophole where regional rules differed.
Creates a rebuttable presumption that shark fins on a fishing vessel came from finning, so enforcement does not depend on catching a crew in the act of dumping a body.
Bars imports of sharks and shark fins from any country that lacks anti-finning and data rules comparable to U.S. rules, so foreign fleets cannot simply export their finning to the U.S. market.

Requires annual reports identifying nations whose vessels practice finning, and directs the Commerce and State Departments to negotiate bilateral, regional, and United Nations agreements toward an international finning ban.

Funds research on shark populations, gear that avoids accidental shark catch, and survival after release, including a cooperative research program with the commercial longline industry in the Western Pacific.

analysis.who_pays: Shark-finning operations and shark fin traders, who profit by taking only the high-value fins (fins are about 5 percent of a shark's weight but the most lucrative part) and discarding the rest. Importers of foreign shark fins would also face new certification requirements, and fishing vessels would bear documentation and release-handling burdens.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shark finning operations and fin traders

drawbacks.text: The bill presumes that fins found on a fishing vessel were taken by finning, and while operators can rebut the presumption with observer and dockside-inspection records, the burden of proof falls on honest vessels that catch sharks legally.

The import certification regime could restrict shark product trade and adds administrative work for the Commerce Department and foreign suppliers, and enforcement of landing rules in remote Pacific fisheries is genuinely difficult.

The bill's own findings concede that a U.S.-only ban would not stop finning by foreign fleets, which were landing roughly 180 metric tons of fins through U.S. Pacific vessels and ports each year, so domestic action alone would only partly address the problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation gains — ending a practice that wastes about 95 percent of every finned shark and protecting slow-reproducing species from collapse — outweigh the compliance costs for fishers, which the bill tries to soften through rebuttable presumption procedures, observer documentation, and cooperative research with the longline industry. The honest weakness is scale: a domestic ban alone cannot save migratory shark populations without the international agreements the bill directs the government to pursue.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2000, and the committee never acted on it before the 106th Congress ended, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kerry introduced the Shark Conservation Act of 2000 on June 29, 2000, joined by Sen. Hollings, and delivered introductory remarks the same day.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, no House counterpart recorded in the action history — appears before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shark-finning operations and fin traders benefited from the bill's death, because no national finning ban or import restriction was enacted in that Congress; consumers and shark populations gained nothing from the bill itself.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shark finning operators and fin traders

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 29, 2000 and took no further action — no hearing or committee vote — before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican ever acted on the bill in the record; with no hearings or votes, no partisan pattern of support or opposition is visible.

industries.industry: Shark finning operations and shark fin traders
industries.note: The bill outlaws finning — taking only the lucrative fins (about 5 percent of a shark's weight) and dumping the rest — and bans imports of fins from countries that allow it. Its profits depend on a practice that wastes most of the animal and drives overfishing, which works against the public's interest in sustainable oceans.

Vessels would face new documentation, landing, and shark-release requirements, but the bill also funds a cooperative research program with the longline industry and research on market development for legally caught sharks.
Importers would need certification that foreign harvests meet U.S.-comparable anti-finning standards, cutting off uncertified supply.
